en: He was a hero beyond all other mortals.
All was complete in him.
Your father Manas—
He was the lion who served him.
When your father could barely endure,
For your fierce-maned father Manas,
Throwing the whole world into confusion,
As he served your father,
The khwajas in white turbans,
‘For Manas, my father's sworn brother,
They will not recite the Qur’an,’ he said.
He bound them with their turbans.
Some sixty khwajas
He slaughtered and laid low.
The forty ishans of Andizhan
He beat with a whip,
Made them all run on foot,
Made them say, ‘We submit, elder brother!’
Made them taste suffering while alive,
Inflicted mighty torment on them,
Hung saddlebags about their necks,
He broke whoever he met,
Beat the forty ishans,
And made them serve your father.
Ak Eshen in Mecca
He had brought within five days.
Khans Koshoi and Toshtuk,
‘At the games for Manas, my father's sworn brother,
I shall stake them as prizes,’ he said.
Abyke and Kobosh, all six,
‘As the prize for the second horse,
I shall stake these six,’ he said,
And left them all helpless.
When your father was gravely ill,
He was the warrior who served him.
Felled in his flowering days,
He was the lion who spared nothing.
‘I shall not stand idly by,’ he said.
‘For Manas, my father's sworn brother,
I shall gather all the surrounding people.
The people who obey me
I shall honor as guests.
If any people will not obey,
I shall use force against them.
Those who fall into my hands,
For Manas, my father's sworn brother,
I shall slaughter as sacrifices,’ he said,
And began to wreak turmoil.
When your father Manas died,
Unable to endure his wrath,
All the people
Were nearly wiped out.
His fine mustache smoothed,
Clouding my eyes blessed by Kydyr,
My only one, my magnanimous Manas,
Set out toward Judgment Day.
‘Alas, Manas, take me with you!’
Lamenting with ringing cries,
Khan Koshoi wept and wailed.
Kissing the back of his hand,
Koshoi came to bid farewell.
Eleman's brave Toshtuk,
Zhamgyrchy of the Eshtek,
They too came to bid farewell.
Urumkan's Kokboru
Then lamented with ringing cries:
‘Matchless Manas, my warrior friend,
Do not leave me behind you.
Take me with you, my friend!’
All the giants said farewell.
They stood holding hands,
Saying, ‘Farewell, farewell!’
As they stood holding hands,
Your khan father Manas closed his eyes.
When he set out for the next world,
Your lion father blessed by Kydyr,
When he departed toward Judgment Day,
Koenaly of the young forelock,
The boy kept struggling.
‘To Manas, my father's sworn brother,
I shall say farewell,’ he said.
The boy would not stop wrenching free.
Poor Kanykei was in distress.
The boy Koenaly,
Kanykei would not let him go.
When she seized him as he struggled,
Your saintly mother, ah, Kanykei,
Pondered and spoke:
‘My cherished foal,
Khan Manas, your father's sworn brother,
Was complete in every way.
He was a warrior protected by Shai.
He was a mighty conqueror.
His eyes held deadly power.
Manas, your father's sworn brother—
The deadly power has not left his eyes;
The radiance of his face has not yet gone out.
Khan Manas, your father's sworn brother,
If he fixes his gaze on you, my foal, it will go ill with you.
Even one look will bring you harm.
Ah, stop, my son, stop!’ she said.
As Kanykei held him,
The boy said:
‘Ah, my aunt Kanykei!
Khan Manas, my father's sworn brother—
Is my life worth more than Manas's?
With most magnanimous Manas
Let me go too.
If he will take me, here I am.
Let me remain Manas's companion.’
So saying, the young-forelocked boy
His motherly Kanykei
Shook off and flung from his arm.
A hero such as Manas,
He rushed up and took by the hand.
Then the young boy
Gripped him tightly.
Mighty Manas regained his speech,
And opened his eyes.
‘Ever since I have been Manas,
Infidels and Muslims
I have driven and oppressed.
I, the fierce-maned one, have fought with many;
My poor head has brushed against many lands.
I have clashed with many giants,
Fought with many giants.
In all the world, anything like this,
Poor soul, I have never seen.
The boy's eyes are burning coals.
His grip strikes hard as a bullet.
He has no equal in all the world.
Ah, his twelve limbs are in perfect balance.
The boy is twelve years old.
This little people of Islam,
Without bringing sorrow to the Muslims,
He is a warrior you should cherish, my people!
No enemy who meets this boy will fare well.
No one who encounters him will remain unharmed.
The boy wears a garment with a silken weft.
Whose cloth might this be?
Ah, he is a lion unique among mankind.
Whose son might this boy be?’
As the bloodthirsty one spoke thus,
Then that noble woman Kanykei
Spoke words of mourning:
‘Ah, bloodthirsty one, on all your journeys,
And now when you are about to depart,
Incorrigible fierce-maned one, you have not changed.
Warrior, you have not given up your greed.
My bloodthirsty one, wherever you go,
Warrior, you mean to leave suffering behind!
All the warriors you encounter,
Warrior, unwilling to leave them to others,
My fierce-maned one, you mean to take them with you!
My fierce-maned one, if you ask about this boy,
A spring flowing down from the hills,
He is the son of your sworn brother,
Kokboru's dear Koenaaly.’
Ah, when Kanykei said this,
Khan Manas grew sorrowful.
‘Ah, Kanykei, you cunning woman,
You know my precious secret.
My blood-red, radiant face—
You did not show him when its light had faded,
When my strength had fled,
When it had left my breast, you did not show him.
When my neck had tilted toward the north,
Nor showed him to me when I turned,
My wretched eyes would not open,
Nor showed him to me when they closed.
Alas, my brave son in youthful bloom,
My evil eye has struck him hard.
This child will not last seven days;
Alas, he will not reach maturity.
There was venom in my eyes;
Alas, he will not see next autumn.
Khan Manas found his voice and said:
“O Kokboru, my sworn friend beyond death,
Your only son Koenaaly—
Will you give him to me?” he asked.
“If you give your son to me,
I shall take him as my companion.
At my feet and at my head,
I shall place him to fill the space.”
When Khan Manas asked this,
Kokboru rose and said:
“Khan Manas, take me, let alone my son!
Khan Manas, take my dark black eyes!
Khan Manas, may I perish if I groan!
Khan Manas, if I begrudge my son,
Khan Manas, if I hurt your feelings,
Khan Manas, take my many people in Crimea!
Khan Manas, take me along with my son!
Khan Manas, take the village pitched upon my land!
Along with my son, Khan Manas,
Take my wife from my home!
Khan Manas, leave two of us and take one!
Khan Manas, leave the others and take me!
Let alone my son, my dearest friend,
I would not begrudge you my life.
Manas, I give you my son.
Giving my son, I send you,
Khan Manas, my greeting for the hereafter!”
Kokboru said this three times,
Crying out loudly and forcefully.
The wolf-maned leopard Manas
Had his wish fulfilled:
The only son born of his body
Kokboru gave to his friend.
Then the giants Koshoi and Toshtuk wept,
Kanykei and Bakai all wept:
“Alas, how could he give up his child?”
All who saw it were amazed.
When the Magnanimous One died thus,
Many a mighty man cast earth upon him.
When they buried Khan Manas,
Manas's friend Kokboru
Set off toward his own people.
When he departed from Talas,
He traveled seven days without stopping,
Passed through Andijan,
And crossed the Kara-Kum.
Beyond it lay Chambyl-Bel.
When he reached Chambyl-Bel,
He lay down to sleep his fill,
Letting the swift horses graze.
He slept propped upon his elbow,
Resting quietly for a little while.
His tent with golden ties
He spread and pitched upon a hill.
He gave himself to merriment
And rested there without weariness.
The mountain slopes were veiled in haze.
With Zhanaaly, Khan Karach,
That Kokboru
Was an enemy to the death.
They split gallbladders and cut off heads,
They raided horses, and men died.
The two khans bore a feud;
They took up spears from the ground,
Fought wherever they met,
Rode stallions swift as wind,
Fought crying, “O my spiritual patron!”
A dreadful battle took place.
Young Koenaaly, the dear boy,
Had not fought with gunfire,
Had not settled far away;
That boy, to his father,
Had given no aid by striking with his whip.
The young topknotted boy lay naked;
The Turkmens had come swarming in,
With pale mottled pennants and banners,
With an uproar of “Boy-boy!”
When the unforeseen battle broke out,
That boy came out naked,
Gripped a spear and broke the ranks.
